title: Humility of the fourth Guru
hookLine: tradition says Guru Ram Das answered a visitor's question about his beard by wiping the visitor's feet

cards: Someone you respect comes to visit, a renunciant well-known for his discipline. He looks you up and down and asks, with a small edge, why you've let your beard grow so long. A fair question, or a jab?
There are easy answers: explain yourself, laugh it off, ask a question back. Why Sikhs keep their hair uncut came up earlier on this path; today's story is about the answer, not the hair.
Sikh tradition tells it of Guru Ram Das, and his answer wasn't a word at all.

teach.b: The visitor, tradition says, was Baba Sri Chand, the son of Guru Nanak, a respected ascetic in his own right, honored by the Udasi sadhus. He came to see the fourth Guru and asked about his long beard.

teach.h: TO WIPE THE FEET OF HOLY MEN.
teach.b: Guru Ram Das answered: it's for wiping the feet of holy men like you. And then, the story goes, he knelt and began to do it. Three things make this land.
First, he doesn't defend himself. A question with an edge invites an argument; he turns it into an invitation to serve. Second, he serves someone who might have been a rival.
Here is the founder's own son, and the Guru now sitting in the founder's place kneels at his feet. The story is told with honor for both men. Third, the story matches his hymns.

teach.h: WORMS AND INSECTS AT THE GURU'S DOOR.
teach.b: In a hymn that is part of the Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer, Guru Ram Das speaks to the Guru like this, paraphrased: we are like small worms and insects, O True Guru, and we seek your shelter; be kind, and light up the Name in us.
That's not false modesty. It's a Guru who knows that the light he carries isn't his own.
It sits close to the rest of his days: the Guru who asks for the dust of the Gursikh's feet, who builds a city around a pool for everyone, who answers a jab by kneeling.

teach.h: FREE ENOUGH OF YOURSELF TO KNEEL.
teach.b: Humble service, in the stories about him, isn't thinking less of yourself.
It's being free enough of yourself to kneel.

how: Sikhs tell this story of Guru Ram Das and Baba Sri Chand when they speak of humility, and seva, humble service such as cleaning shoes and washing dishes at the gurdwara, is part of Sikh community life.

games.q: what does “humility of the fourth guru” mean?
o: Guru Ram Das wearing plain clothes to hide his rank
Guru Ram Das living alone, away from the sangat
Guru Ram Das kneeling to serve, free of himself

games.q: the story and the hymn: tap the pairs.
p: for wiping the feet of holy men
we are like worms and insects
free enough of yourself to kneel

s: in the story, Guru Ram Das argues with his visitor about the beard
he answers that it's for wiping the feet of holy men, and kneels to do it.
tradition says the visitor was Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's son
a respected ascetic, honored by the Udasi sadhus; the story honors both men.
Guru Ram Das's own hymns sound proud of his station
in the Rehras hymn he says we are like worms and insects, seeking the True Guru's shelter.

games.q: a respected visitor asks, with an edge, why your beard is so long. you're Guru Ram Das. what do you do?
o: say it's for wiping the feet of holy men, and kneel.
ask him why he has none.
games.why: tradition says he answered that way and knelt to wipe the visitor's feet: a jab answered with service.

practice: Look over today and find one job nobody wants, the dishes someone else left, shoes piled at the door, the trash nobody takes out.
Picture yourself doing it slowly, without announcing it or keeping score, and let the breath settle on that picture, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Humility of the fourth Guru. Tradition says that asked about his beard, Guru Ram Das said it was for wiping the feet of holy men, and knelt to do it. Today's word.

orig.note: humility, the Punjabi word Sikhs use for the lowliness the stories of Guru Ram Das show.

carryVoice: Your line: humble service. Nobody needs to know it was you. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition: Guru Ram Das and Baba Sri Chand
Guru Granth Sahib, Gujri Mahala 4, Ang 10, in Rehras (we are like worms and insects, True Guru, we seek your shelter; be kind and light up the Name)
